rows.question: Should we administer the prophylactic antibiotic before skin incision or wait until after the umbilical cord is clamped?

per_sentence.text: Clinical guidelines strongly recommend administering appropriate parenteral prophylactic antimicrobial agents  before skin incision  in all cesarean section procedures (Category IA–strong recommendation; high-quality evidence) .
Prophylactic administration during the  hour before incision  is likely more effective than waiting until cord clamping .

Studies and policy shifts have shown that administering antibiotics before skin incision results in a significant decline/decrease in post-cesarean infectious complications compared to administration at cord clamping .
A meta-analysis showed no clear evidence of harm to the child from this brief antibiotic exposure at birth .
Concern regarding neonatal antibiotic exposure and sepsis led to practices of delaying antibiotics until after the umbilical cord is clamped .

The WHO guidelines ( Managing complications in pregnancy and childbirth ) recommend a single dose of prophylactic antibiotics  after the cord is clamped and cut  , and some literature notes an exception for cesarean section where the initial dose is given immediately after the cord is clamped .

Clinical trials show varied results: one randomized clinical trial (Thigpen et al.) found no difference in maternal infectious complications, neonatal sepsis, or ICU admissions whether given before skin incision or at cord clamping .

While the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommend antibiotic prophylaxis, neither historically made conclusive recommendations regarding timing .

rows.question: My pre-op patient keeps saying she doesn't want to keep taking her blood pressure pills after surgery — what should I be drawing out of her to figure out if she'll actually stay on them?

per_sentence.text: Missed doses:  Ask,  "Have you missed any pills in the past week?"  (A self-report of missing any pills is consistent with an adherence rate of less than 60%) .

Perceptions of medication need, effectiveness, and safety:  Ask,  "How is your blood pressure doing?"  and  "Are you having any problems with your medications?"  to uncover medication-specific barriers such as side effects, the number of daily medications, dosing frequency, taste, duration of treatment, and cost .
"Are you having any trouble getting and taking your medications?"
"Are you able to be regular in your medication taking?"
These explore access issues (e.g., filling prescriptions, getting refills, booking clinic visits, running out of pills) and inconveniences (e.g., carrying medications, using public bathrooms) .
Goals, Pros/Cons, and Discrepancies (Motivational Interviewing)

Treatment goals:  Ask,  "What do you want to happen as a result of taking this medicine for your blood pressure?"  Establishing treatment-related goals gives taking medication a definable purpose and highlights behaviors that do not support those goals .

Important life aspects & priorities:  Elicit short- and long-term goals and aspects of her life that are important to her but could be compromised by untreated blood pressure (such as the fear of having a stroke or losing independence) .
Pros and cons:  Ask about the pros and cons of the needed changes, and repeat them back using reflection to create dissonance/ambivalence .
Source of resistance:  Use reflective listening to explore where her resistance is coming from and why it is there, while ignoring antagonistic elements to focus on underlying issues .
Past strategies:  Ask,  "What worked before?"  or  "What do you think helped you to be successful last time?"  to assess her strengths, resources, and past successes with medication management .

rows.question: If my post-op patient is short of breath and we suspect a PE, do we need a chest X-ray before booking her for a V/Q scan or CTPA, and what's the radiation risk to the baby?

per_sentence.text: Is a Chest X-ray (CXR) needed before booking a V/Q scan or CTPA?
A CXR should be performed before deciding on further diagnostic imaging .
A  normal CXR  prior to V/Q scanning improves the likelihood of obtaining a definitive V/Q result .
If the CXR is  abnormal  and there is clinical suspicion of a PE, a  CTPA should be performed  in preference to a V/Q scan .
(Note: If the patient also has symptoms and signs of a DVT, compression duplex ultrasound should be performed first, as confirming a DVT may make further thoracic radiation imaging unnecessary ).
Chest X-ray:  The radiation dose to the fetus at any stage of pregnancy is negligible (less than  0.01 mSv ) .
Overall Fetal Safety Thresholds:  With both CTPA and V/Q scanning, radiation doses are well below the accepted thresholds for teratogenicity, fetal death, and fetal growth restriction .

The International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) estimates the increased risk of fatal childhood cancer up to age 15 following  in utero  radiation exposure to be  0.006% per mGy  (or  1 in 17,000 per mGy ) .

rows.question: Should we administer the prophylactic antibiotic before skin incision or wait until after the umbilical cord is clamped?

per_sentence.text: Below is a synthesis of the guideline bodies, their positions, points of agreement and difference, and what the text leaves unestablished.

Position:  Recommends administering prophylactic antibiotics prior to skin incision (specifically within 60 minutes, or optimally within 30 to 60 minutes before incision) for all women undergoing caesarean sections (both elective and non-elective).
Rationale:  To establish adequate bactericidal serum and tissue concentrations at the time the incision is made.
Note on Clamping:  WHO acknowledges that evidence supports administration after umbilical cord clamping as well, but it ultimately favors pre-incision timing.

Pre-incision Position:  In general surgical prophylaxis guidance and several caesarean section references (e.g., CDC T1 p3, p1/p8), the CDC recommends administering parenteral prophylactic antimicrobials  prior to skin incision  rather than after umbilical cord clamping to effectively prevent surgical site infections (SSIs) and ensure adequate tissue concentrations.

Post-clamping Position:  Alternatively, specific CDC guidance (CDC T1, p13) advises/recommends administering the prophylactic dose  immediately after umbilical cord clamping  in high-risk caesarean sections.
Position:  Aligns with administering prophylactic antibiotics within 60 minutes prior to skin incision to ensure adequate tissue concentrations at incision time.

rows.question: Are we required to mandate that every patient shower with an antiseptic agent before their operation, or is standard soap acceptable?

Patients can perform a full-body bath or shower with either standard soap (antimicrobial or non-antimicrobial) or an antiseptic agent at least the night before surgery, with no stated preference between the two.

rows.question: Our ergometrine vials have been sitting in the theatre drug cupboard at room temperature — is that okay to give for PPH prevention, or do we need to switch to something else?

per_sentence.text: Ergometrine is heat-sensitive and strictly relies on cold-chain storage.

Carbetocin  (100 µg IM/IV) is the recommended alternative for vaginal or caesarean births if oxytocin is unavailable or its quality cannot be guaranteed.
Oxytocin  is the agent of choice for third-stage prophylaxis (specifically 5 IU slow IV for caesarean section).
Carbetocin  (100 µg IV bolus) is recommended for elective caesarean sections.
WHO and RCOG agree that  oxytocin is the primary drug of choice  for PPH prophylaxis, and both endorse  carbetocin  as an appropriate alternative.

RCOG  specifies dosing for caesarean delivery (5 IU slow IV oxytocin) and explicitly recommends carbetocin (100 µg IV bolus) specifically for elective caesarean sections.

per_sentence.text: RCOG:  Cephalosporins and carbapenems (including ceftriaxone) are  strictly contraindicated  if the patient has a history of anaphylaxis to penicillins or a severe beta-lactam allergy.
WHO:  Specifically warns that cephalosporins and carbapenems (such as imipenem) can trigger anaphylaxis in patients with a prior anaphylactic or immediate reaction to penicillin.
CDC:  Highlights that patients must be screened for cross-reactivity or intolerance before using a cephalosporin substitute, as cephalosporins may be unsuitable depending on the allergy profile.
RCOG:  Notes that cephalosporins may still serve as an alternative in  certain  beta-lactam-allergic patients (i.e., those without a history of severe/anaphylactic reactions).
Gram-Positive Coverage:   Vancomycin ,  clindamycin , or  teicoplanin  can replace beta-lactams ( CDC, WHO ).
Vancomycin  is specifically indicated in cases of severe penicillin allergy ( RCOG ).
Combination Regimens:   Clindamycin plus gentamicin  is recommended as an alternative regimen for pelvic infections and endometritis ( WHO, RCOG ).
RCOG:  For life-threatening puerperal sepsis, recommended empirical therapy includes  meropenem plus clindamycin  (with  vancomycin  added if MRSA is suspected or in patients with a history of MRSA).
Note:  Meropenem is a carbapenem and is only viable if carbapenems are not ruled out by a history of anaphylaxis/severe beta-lactam allergy.
Piperacillin-tazobactam is explicitly contraindicated in beta-lactam allergy.
NICE, RCOG, OpenRN:  Require prompt administration of broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within  1 hour  of sepsis recognition or shock diagnosis.
OpenRN:  Blood cultures should be drawn prior to antibiotic administration to guide subsequent therapy.
The  WHO, RCOG, and CDC  agree that a prior severe or anaphylactic reaction to penicillin presents a cross-reactivity risk that contraindicates the use of cephalosporins and carbapenems.
NICE, RCOG, and OpenRN  agree on the necessity of rapid, broad-spectrum IV antimicrobial coverage within 1 hour for suspected high-risk sepsis.
CDC, WHO, and RCOG  agree on non-beta-lactam agents such as vancomycin and clindamycin as core substitutes for patients who cannot receive penicillins.

RCOG  identifies cephalosporins and carbapenems (meropenem) as potential empiric options for specific beta-lactam-allergic patients or life-threatening sepsis, whereas  WHO  places stronger emphasis on the absolute contraindication of both cephalosporins and imipenem in those with prior anaphylactic reactions.

Certain sources in the material explicitly state that specific alternative regimens and cross-reactivity determinations for beta-lactam allergy in maternal sepsis remain  not established  within those specific texts.

The material does not detail non-beta-lactam alternatives specifically for carbapenem-contraindicated patients with septic shock outside of the clindamycin-gentamicin and vancomycin/teicoplanin mentions.

sentences: Based on the provided guidelines from the  CDC, WHO, RCOG, NICE, and OpenRN , here is how to determine cross-reactivity risks and select alternative antimicrobial therapy for a septic post-operative patient with a documented penicillin allergy.
Determining if Cephalosporins or Carbapenems are Ruled Out
RCOG:  Cephalosporins and carbapenems (including ceftriaxone) are  strictly contraindicated  if the patient has a history of anaphylaxis to penicillins or a severe beta-lactam allergy.
WHO:  Specifically warns that cephalosporins and carbapenems (such as imipenem) can trigger anaphylaxis in patients with a prior anaphylactic or immediate reaction to penicillin.
CDC:  Highlights that patients must be screened for cross-reactivity or intolerance before using a cephalosporin substitute, as cephalosporins may be unsuitable depending on the allergy profile.
RCOG:  Notes that cephalosporins may still serve as an alternative in  certain  beta-lactam-allergic patients (i.e., those without a history of severe/anaphylactic reactions).
What to Administer Instead
Gram-Positive Coverage:   Vancomycin ,  clindamycin , or  teicoplanin  can replace beta-lactams ( CDC, WHO ).
Vancomycin  is specifically indicated in cases of severe penicillin allergy ( RCOG ).
Combination Regimens:   Clindamycin plus gentamicin  is recommended as an alternative regimen for pelvic infections and endometritis ( WHO, RCOG ).
RCOG:  For life-threatening puerperal sepsis, recommended empirical therapy includes  meropenem plus clindamycin  (with  vancomycin  added if MRSA is suspected or in patients with a history of MRSA).
Note:  Meropenem is a carbapenem and is only viable if carbapenems are not ruled out by a history of anaphylaxis/severe beta-lactam allergy.
Piperacillin-tazobactam is explicitly contraindicated in beta-lactam allergy.
NICE, RCOG, OpenRN:  Require prompt administration of broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within  1 hour  of sepsis recognition or shock diagnosis.
OpenRN:  Blood cultures should be drawn prior to antibiotic administration to guide subsequent therapy.
Agreements and Differences
The  WHO, RCOG, and CDC  agree that a prior severe or anaphylactic reaction to penicillin presents a cross-reactivity risk that contraindicates the use of cephalosporins and carbapenems.
NICE, RCOG, and OpenRN  agree on the necessity of rapid, broad-spectrum IV antimicrobial coverage within 1 hour for suspected high-risk sepsis.
CDC, WHO, and RCOG  agree on non-beta-lactam agents such as vancomycin and clindamycin as core substitutes for patients who cannot receive penicillins.

RCOG  identifies cephalosporins and carbapenems (meropenem) as potential empiric options for specific beta-lactam-allergic patients or life-threatening sepsis, whereas  WHO  places stronger emphasis on the absolute contraindication of both cephalosporins and imipenem in those with prior anaphylactic reactions.
What the Material Does Not Establish
The provided text does not provide a specific diagnostic protocol or standardized screening tool to determine cross-reactivity in clinical practice.
